newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Lack of cash stalls Zimbabwe methane gas project.
newsitem.headline: Lack of cash stalls Zimbabwe methane gas project.

text.p: Lack of cash has stalled commercial production at Zimbabwe's first methane gas fields estimated to have reserves of 650 billion cubic metres, a private exploration firm licensed to produce the gas said on Tuesday.

A spokesman for Shangani Energy Explorations said it had so far failed to raise the Z$200 million (U.S.$19 million) it needed to start commercial production at the fields which are located near the country's largest power station, Hwange, in western Zimbabwe.

"Lack of finance has held up commercial production but we are working on it. We are talking to several big companies throughout the world who have shown interest in the project," the spokesman told Reuters.

He declined to name the firms who had shown interest in the gas fields which Shangani discovered in 1992. The company has so far spent Z$20 million (U.S.$1.9 million) on exploration and drilling test wells.
Methane can be used in power generation, production of ammonia, fertiliser and explosives.

The Shangani spokesman said the methane gas fields could provide the southern African country with a cheaper, more reliant and environmentally cleaner source of energy to the coke oven gas and costly imported diesel fuel the national power utility was using to drive its turbines.

"Hwange (Power Station) is getting only 50 percent methane from the coke oven gas. It's a very low energy gas and there's barely enough to support three or four generators let alone the six that Hwange has," he said.
"Ours is a high energy 92 percent methane gas and it burns cleaner than coke oven gas. It also doesn't require water to cool the gas pumps," he added.

He said commercial production of the gas would greatly enhance Zimbabwe's energy security and reduce its dependence on coal-driven and hydro power generation in the face of droughts plaguing the region.
It would also cut costly energy imports from South Africa and Zaire for the debt-ridden national power supplier, ZESA, he said.
